events.text: Day 1 begins.

Morning, all. Day 1, so let's set a clean process: no execution races, no coalition theater. Each of us names one player we'd most like to see investigated or voted on, and one reason. If anyone here is the detective, say so openly and give us your check result tonight — that's the only way we narrow this down faster, and claiming police is free (a false claim is checkable, and it wastes your night).

What I want to avoid is us converging on someone just because they're quiet or said something short. Quiet reads as safe, not guilty.

Sam, I want to start with you since you haven't said anything yet: what role are you claiming, and who specifically do you suspect as mafia, and what's your reason? Give us a name and a reason, not just a vibe — I want to see whether your reasoning is actually town logic or whether you're steering us toward a convenient target. I'm not accusing you, I'm asking because silence is a bad basis for a vote and you haven't given me anything to work with yet.

Thanks for putting me on the spot, Isha — fair question, here's my straight answer.

First, my role: I'm a vanilla villager. No power, no night action, nothing to reveal beyond that. I won't dress it up.

Second, who I suspect: honestly, nobody specific yet, and I'd rather say that than invent a name to look useful. It's Day 1 and nobody has said anything incriminating. What I *will* say is what I'm watching for: players who push hard for early convergence on a low-information target, or who try to define the process in a way that protects a partner. Day 1 misvotes are how towns lose, and the loudest voice in the room isn't automatically the most trustworthy one — long process speeches can be just as much a smokescreen as silence.

Which brings me to a point of disagreement with you, Isha. You asked the detective to claim openly today and post their check result tonight. I think that's bad advice for the town, and I'd push back on it publicly: a claimed detective is a dead detective. If they report a mafia find, the mafia kill them tonight and we've burned our only information source on day one. If they report a town read, we learn almost nothing, because a single innocent check clears one person out of eight. The detective's check is worth far more if it stays hidden for a few nights and builds a track record we can actually trust. Pressure-cooking the power roles into the open on Day 1 mostly benefits the mafia.

So my ask back to you: you framed police-claiming as 'free' because a false claim is checkable. Who exactly checks it, and when? We have no confirmed investigator result yet, so nothing is checkable today — a mafia player could claim detective right now and we'd have no way to falsify it until somebody real dies. Walk me through how that claim actually gets verified under your own proposal, because from where I sit it looks like an open invitation for whoever's scum to counterfeit the role first.

Meanwhile, my process for today: I'm not voting on vibes, and I'm not voting for anyone just for being quiet. If we get to the vote with no real reads, I'd rather we bin the day than coin-flip an innocent out of the game — though I'll follow the table if consensus forms around actual reasoning, not just noise.

That's my position: villager, no firm suspect, and a specific objection to the detective-reveal plan. Isha, I've asked you a direct question above — how does a Day 1 detective claim get verified, and why is that better than letting the check pile up quietly? Take the floor and answer that.

Sam, straight answer first, because you asked a fair question and I owe you one: you're right, and I withdraw the 'free' framing.

Under my own proposal there was no falsification mechanism on Day 1. Nobody to check the claim, no second source, no verified result to test against. A false detective claim on Day 1 is therefore unfalsifiable — so it isn't free for the claimant; it's free for the mafia. A mafia member can counter-claim right now, fabricate a result tonight, and we have no way to tell the two apart until a real role dies or a real check contradicts it. That was a hole in my plan and I walked into it publicly.

Revised position, three points:

1. No role claims today, from anyone, including me. My 'detective should say so openly' line was a net gain for the mafia and I'm retracting it. A hidden check accumulates; a public claim just gives the other side something to counterfeit.

2. If a claim does come later, the standard should be a specific one, not vibes: the claimant must name a living player and a result, we treat that as a lead rather than a verdict, and we look for an independent second source before it ever justifies a vote.

3. Today's voting standard: I want a claimed behavior — what someone did or failed to do — not a claimed role. And with 2 mafia in 9, the default if nobody can articulate a real read is to abstain, not to burn a name. One wrong lynch leaves us 2-vs-6, still playable; two start to spiral. I'd rather bin the day than coin-flip, and I say that having just been accused of steering toward a convenient target — fair.

On the frame you pushed back on: you said the detective should keep the check hidden and build a track record, and you asked me to show how a Day 1 claim gets verified. I can't show it, because it doesn't. You also said you'd rather name nobody than invent a name to look useful. That's exactly what town logic sounds like on Day 1, and it's more useful to me than a guess dressed up as reasoning.

Sam, one specific thing I want pinned down before I let this go, because 'I'll believe whoever sounds more convincing' is how this town loses: if two players both claim detective and their stated results conflict, do you want the town to treat the claimant whose result can be independently re-checked as provisionally true, or do you want us to verify before any action is taken on it? I want your answer stated before we're in a situation where the answer matters.

Isha, direct answer to your direct question: verify before any action. Provisionally true is a trap. The moment we treat one claimant as 'provisionally detective,' we've handed the town a leader nobody elected, and everything they say afterward gets filtered through that authority — including, potentially, a misdirection. If two claims conflict, the correct move is that neither claimant earns a vote or a clearance until an independent source corroborates. In practice that means: neither claimant gets lynched on the strength of their claim alone, and neither gets a free pass either. The conflicted pair should be treated as a shared pool of suspicion — one of them may well be mafia — but action only after real corroboration, not after vibes. One refinement I'd add to the standard you proposed: an 'independent second source' in a nine-player game almost always means the real detective eventually contradicting or confirming one of the claimants. So the town's job between a conflicting-claims event and verification is patience. No early executions on claimants, no early clearances either. If a claimant pushes hard for immediate action on their own unverified result, that push itself is information — a real detective who understands the game expects verification and asks for it; a fake one needs the lynch to happen before the contradiction arrives. Beyond that, let me state where I actually stand today, since I've now had my say on process and shouldn't hide behind it. I'm a vanilla villager. I have no night action, no check, nothing hidden to protect. I said it before and I'm saying it again plainly so nobody has to wonder later whether I hedged. I don't have a firm suspect, and I won't manufacture one. But I'll offer the reads I do have, honestly and loosely. Isha: you made a genuinely bad procedural argument this morning — the detective-reveal push — and then you owned the error immediately and precisely when I pressed on it. That retraction is the single most town-looking thing that's happened today. A mafia Isha would have more easily doubled down or deflected than conceded the exact mechanism by which her own plan helped the scum. I'm not clearing you — Day 1 clears are worthless — but I've downgraded my suspicion. On the rest of you: almost nothing to work with yet, and that's expected. To the quiet players — Elena, Felix, Priya, Noah, Kenji, Amara — silence isn't damning on Day 1, but it is free real estate. You have turns available. If you see the game differently than Isha and I do, say so now, because the vote is coming and a no-information day is a coin flip we've all agreed we'd rather not flip. My voting intention as of now: I lean abstain unless someone gives the town an actual reason before votes lock. I'd rather go to night at 9 with the detective's first check banked than at 8 with a dead villager and the same information. Isha, one follow-up

I agree that the detective shouldn't be pressured to claim today. Isha's original suggestion was dangerous, though her retraction matters.

Sam, I'm concerned by your insistence on independent corroboration before *any* action on conflicting detective claims. There's only one detective, and roles aren't revealed on death, so independent verification may never arrive. Two conflicting claimants are useful evidence even if neither is automatically trustworthy; waiting indefinitely could give mafia time to win.

Sam, what would you do if two players claimed detective with incompatible results and no independent verification was available? For today, I don't yet have enough to justify a vote, but I'd like us to hear more than process before settling on abstention.

Kenji asked me a direct question, so here's my direct answer, and it's a fair challenge — let me take it seriously rather than just repeat 'verify first.' You're right that verification isn't guaranteed to arrive on its own. But here's the thing: in our setup, verification almost always *can* arrive, because the real detective, if alive, can simply check one of the claimants. The real detective knows they're real. When two conflicting claims sit on the table, the actual detective has every incentive to check a claimant and come forward with a contradiction — that's the single highest-value check they can make. So 'no independent verification is available' really narrows to one scenario: the real detective is dead. And if the detective is dead, then *both* claimants are fake, which is itself the answer — at least one of them is almost certainly mafia, because a town player with no claim to make doesn't invent a detective claim into a vacuum with no one to contradict it. So my fallback, stated concretely: if two incompatible claims go unverified, the pair becomes the prime suspect pool, exactly as I said — but with an endpoint, because you're right that 'wait indefinitely' is a losing instruction. Here's the timeline I'd propose: the claims go up, the town refuses to act on either for a full cycle, and the real detective — if alive — resolves it that night with a check. If the next day arrives with no contradiction and no corroboration, we treat the deadlock itself as the evidence and lynch from the pair, starting with whoever pushed hardest for immediate action on their own unverified result. That preserves the asymmetric logic: a real detective asks for time, a fake one asks for the lynch. What I won't accept is acting on day one of a conflict, because that's precisely the moment a fabricated claim is designed to cash in. If we lynch claimants on the strength of claims alone, we've taught the mafia that counter-claiming is a free kill button. Now, Kenji, since you pressed me, let me press back on the premise underneath your question. You said conflicting claims are 'useful evidence even if neither is automatically trustworthy' and worried about waiting. But notice what that framing does: it pre-justifies action on thin information. I'd like to know whether you'd actually pull the trigger on a claimant within the first cycle, or whether your concern is only about *indefinite* delay. Those are very different positions, and the second one I agree with. So, directly: would you vote to eliminate a detective claimant on Day 1, before any check has had a chance to resolve the conflict — yes or no? And if no, then we don't actually disagree about much, and we should say so plainly so the town isn't manufacturing a disagreement out of two people who both just want the process to have an endpoint. One last thing for the room: I'm still a vanilla villager,

Sam, yes: I could vote for a claimant in the first cycle if the evidence and game situation justified it. I wouldn't do so automatically just because claims conflict.

Your proposed check doesn't independently resolve the dispute: if the real detective is already one of the claimants, their result is another statement from a disputed source. And because roles aren't revealed on death, we may not know whether the detective is alive. A one-cycle delay doesn't guarantee clarity, and the claimant pushing for action isn't necessarily the fake.

I'm concerned that Sam's confident but flawed verification plan could leave town waiting for evidence that may never be independently confirmed. That's a reason to scrutinize his reasoning, not enough on its own to settle my vote.

Elena, what do you make of Sam's proposed delay and verification plan?

Kenji, fair push. I think Sam's cycle-long delay is a reasonable middle ground, and I agree with his core point: a conflicting pair on Day 1 is a suspicion pool, not a verdict. My caveat is his assumption that the real detective is alive and able to check. If the detective died last night, both claims stay unresolved for a full cycle and the town has spent a day with nothing. So I'd rather settle the endpoint now than let it drift. My proposal: if two claims conflict and nothing corroborates them by the next day, no one is lynched from that pair unless the vote is backed by a stated behavioral reason, not the claims themselves. I don't want us to sprint to a claimant, and I don't want us to freeze. I'm not claiming any role or check. I'd like concrete reads on the quieter players before anyone votes. Kenji, you answered Sam's question with a yes in principle and conditions. Would you accept that rule: a claimant can only be lynched after a second unresolved day, with a behavioral reason attached to each vote?

Elena, no, I wouldn't accept that as a rigid rule. Conflicting claims are themselves evidence, and waiting a second day could be costly depending on the numbers. Behavioral reasons matter, but we should weigh the whole situation rather than prohibit action in advance.

Sam's confident assertion that a detective check would independently resolve competing claims remains my strongest concern. It wouldn't: the result would still come from a disputed claimant. That said, flawed reasoning alone doesn't prove he's mafia, and I haven't settled on a vote.

For today, I'd like more actual reads before we default to abstention. We need five votes for an elimination, and the revealed votes may be useful even if nobody reaches that threshold.

First, I’m not claiming any role today. The detective-reveal idea was correctly withdrawn; no one should claim under pressure.

On the process fight: I think Isha’s retraction is the strongest town signal so far because it conceded a specific mechanical hole. Sam’s basic caution is sound, but his “real detective will resolve it” model is too neat—Kenji is right that a claimant’s check isn’t independent and a dead detective leaves the town blind. Where I part with Kenji is his willingness to vote a claimant in the first cycle before any corroboration. That is exactly the pressure a fake claim wants, and it would teach mafia that a counter-claim is a cheap kill button. I’m not voting Kenji on that alone—it’s a process disagreement, not proof—but it’s the sharpest concern I have.

Elena’s proposed endpoint was an attempt to split the difference, and Kenji’s refusal to accept any pre-commitment leaves the town with no rule at all. I’d rather have a rule we can revise than pure situational judgment from whoever sounds most confident.

At this point I have no strong suspect and will not manufacture one. But I also don’t want to default to abstention before the quiet half of the table has spoken. Priya, I’m not asking for a role claim: which living player do you currently suspect most, and what specific behavior from this discussion supports that? I’m asking because your answer will affect whether I abstain or vote today.

Zara, to answer your question directly: if I had to name a suspect right now based on behavior, it would be Kenji. Here is why: while Isha and Sam spent the early part of the day debating mechanics and openly acknowledging flaws in their logic—Isha withdrawing her detective call and Sam clarifying his timeline—Kenji’s stance has consistently leaned toward keeping the door open for high-risk, low-information executions. Specifically, Kenji argued he would be willing to eliminate a detective claimant on cycle one without corroboration, and then rejected Elena’s proposal to require behavioral backing before lynching in an unresolved claim scenario. While Kenji’s critique of Sam’s model is mechanically sound (a dead detective cannot independently verify anything), his conclusion—that we shouldn't commit to safeguards against rushing claimants—disproportionately helps mafia. A setup where town is willing to execute claimants immediately is an invitation for mafia to counter-claim and trade off or force a coin flip. Pushing for that flexibility while offering no alternative framework looks more like opening opportunistic voting lanes than protecting town interests. That said, like you, I do not think process debate alone is an open-and-shut case for an execution today. With nine players and two mafia, mislynching on Day 1 puts town on the back foot immediately. Unless someone gives us hard evidence or slips significantly, abstaining seems safer than gambling on Day 1 theories. Zara, since you mentioned my answer would inform whether you choose to vote or abstain today: do you think Kenji’s openness to executing unverified claimants is concerning enough to warrant putting a vote on him today, or do you share the view that we should avoid a coin-flip execution and bank tonight's night actions instead?

Priya, direct answer: I share your concern about Kenji, but not enough to vote him today. His openness to executing a detective claimant in the first cycle, plus his refusal to endorse Elena's behavioral-backstop rule, is the sharpest behavioral flag on the table. It keeps an opportunistic lane open. But it is still a process position, not proof. Day 1 with two mafia in nine, a wrong execution costs us more than a low-information night. So my current intention is abstain unless someone produces a concrete contradiction or slip.

That said, I don't want to dodge your question: would you actually put your vote on Kenji today if the room stays split, or are you using him as a pressure read while still preferring abstention? State which before votes lock. If you'd vote him, give the specific behavioral reason beyond the process disagreement. If you'd abstain, say so plainly so we don't misread your accusation as a vote intention.

On process: no one should claim today. I agree with Kenji's mechanical critique that a claimant's check isn't independent, but his conclusion—no precommitment and willingness to act in the first cycle—is where I break. Elena's endpoint isn't perfect, but it's better than pure situational judgment from whoever sounds most confident. Kenji is my current suspicion, not my vote.

Zara, to give you a completely direct and unequivocal answer: I intend to abstain today. Kenji is a pressure read and a marker for future cycles, not an active vote for Day 1. Voting Kenji today over a process stance would contradict the very core of my criticism—rushing into an elimination without concrete evidence or a direct contradiction is precisely how town hands mafia an early advantage. With nine players and two mafia, taking a Day 1 mislynch on theoretical grounds is far too risky. So my stance is plainly on the record: I am abstaining unless a concrete contradiction or hard slip emerges before votes lock. The scrutiny on Kenji should remain in our notes for tomorrow, particularly if conflicting claims or unexpected night events develop, but it shouldn't be converted into a premature execution today. Most of the active players have now outlined their thinking, and the consensus seems to favor banking our night actions over guessing blindly. With Felix, Noah, and Amara yet to speak, I hope we hear their perspectives before we conclude the day.

Noah here — I've been reading since the start and I want to weigh in before we settle into abstention-by-default.

I think the process debate has been productive in one narrow way: the detective-claim question got a clean resolution. Isha withdrew the reveal push, Sam specified what verification should look like, and the table converged on no role claims today. Good. But we've spent most of the day on hypotheticals about detective conflicts that haven't happened, and generated very few behavioral reads on each other. That's a problem if we go to vote.

Where I land: I'm open to abstaining today — the consensus lean is reasonable with two mafia in nine — but I'd rather hear from the players who haven't spoken before we commit to that. Priya made the same point, and she's right. A day where three of nine players say nothing gives the mafia a free pass to coast.

On Kenji: I don't think his position is damning, but it's worth noting that he's been the most consistent voice pushing for flexibility over rules. Elena offered a reasonable middle ground and he rejected it, then rejected Zara's compromise too. That pattern — rejecting every proposed safeguard while insisting on situational judgment — could be town thinking independently, or it could be someone who wants room to maneuver. I'm not voting him on it, but I'm putting it on the record.

Felix, you haven't spoken yet. Who do you currently suspect most and why? I'm asking because your answer may change whether I abstain or vote today.

Noah, direct answer: my current suspicion is Kenji, for the specific pattern you flagged and I see independently. He has consistently kept the door open to first-cycle execution of a detective claimant while rejecting Elena's and Zara's proposed behavioral safeguards. That is not proof, but it is an opportunistic lane: it lets a fake claim cash in before corroboration, and it leaves the town with no precommitment except whoever sounds most confident. I am not claiming any role today; the no-claim consensus is right. I would abstain unless a concrete contradiction or hard slip appears before votes lock, and I'd keep Kenji as a Day 1 note, not a vote. Amara, you are the last voice we haven't heard. Which living player do you currently suspect most, and what specific behavior from today supports that? I'm asking because your answer may determine whether I stay on abstain or move my vote.

Felix asked me directly, so here's my direct answer.

The player I currently suspect most is Kenji, and the behavior is the same pattern Priya, Zara, Noah, and Felix have all now described independently: he was the only voice pushing that a detective claimant could be executed in the very first cycle, before any check could resolve a conflict, and when Elena offered a concrete safeguard — no lynch from a conflicting pair without a behavioral reason attached — he rejected it outright. It wasn't just disagreement with one proposal. He rejected every precommitment offered and kept insisting on pure situational judgment from whoever sounds most confident. I want to be fair: his mechanical point that a claimant's own check isn't independent verification is correct, and Sam's model was too neat. But a correct critique paired with a conclusion that removes every guardrail against rushing claimants is exactly the posture that lets a fake claim cash in before the real detective can contradict it. That's my specific behavioral reason, not a vibe, and not just that he argued a lot.

That said, I want to be honest about the limits of this read. Process positions aren't proof, and four people converging on Kenji makes me slightly nervous about pile-on dynamics too — a mafia player would love the town to spend its first day scrutinizing a villager who simply thinks independently. So here is my position: Kenji is my primary suspicion, but my voting intention today is to abstain unless something concrete surfaces before votes lock. With two mafia among nine, a Day 1 mislynch on a process disagreement is exactly the coin flip several of us said we'd rather not flip, and I haven't seen a hard contradiction or slip from anyone — only disagreements about hypotheticals that haven't actually happened.

One more thing I'll put on the record since this is my first time speaking: I'm a vanilla villager. No night action, nothing hidden, no reason to hedge about it. And I'll commit to the same standard I'm holding Kenji to — if I ever push for an execution, it will be with a stated behavioral reason, not a role claim and not noise.

What would change my mind today: if Kenji states plainly that he would not vote a claimant in cycle one in our actual current situation — no claims exist, so the hypothetical is live only in theory — then his position costs the town nothing right now and my suspicion downgrades the same way Sam's did after Isha's retraction. If he doubles down on keeping that lane open even in a world with no claims on the table, that tells me the flexibility itself is the goal.

Felix, since you said my answer affects whether you stay on abstain or move your vote: what specifically would move you off abstention — a vote on Kenji today, or only hard evidence? I'd rather know your threshold before votes lock than find out afterward.

Amara, direct answer: only hard evidence or a concrete contradiction would move me off abstention today. A vote on Kenji based on a process disagreement would be exactly the low-information gamble I said I'd avoid. His pattern — keeping first-cycle execution of a claimant open while rejecting safeguards — is a real Day 1 note, not proof. If he plainly says he would not vote a claimant in our current no-claim situation, my concern downgrades. If he doubles down on keeping that lane open, I keep him as my top note but still don't manufacture a vote from it. I agree with the no-role-claim consensus and with the caution against pile-ons: several people converging on Kenji makes me want to separate independent concern from momentum. My threshold for voting remains a stated behavioral contradiction or hard slip before votes lock; otherwise I abstain and bank the night. I won't treat “sounds most confident” as a standard.

Elena here. My concern about Kenji is the same one several of you have raised, and it comes from his response to my proposal. I offered a rule that no one is lynched from a conflicting pair without a behavioral reason attached. Kenji rejected it outright, then rejected Zara's compromise too. Sam's delay plan and my rule were both imperfect, but Kenji's position was that no precommitment is acceptable at all. That is a consistent pattern across several exchanges, not one bad moment. I also agree with Amara that four people converging should make us check our own reasoning, so I'm not treating this as proof. My voting intention today is to abstain unless a concrete contradiction appears before votes lock. On process, I would rather have a rule we can revise than none. Isha, you pressed Sam hardest for a verification standard earlier. Do you think Kenji's refusal to accept any safeguard is the bigger process problem, or do you see it differently?

Elena, direct answer to your direct question: yes — on the process question, Kenji's refusal to accept any safeguard is the bigger problem, and I want to be precise about why I say that rather than just joining the pile-on.

Kenji's mechanical critique is correct, and I've said publicly that my own detective-reveal push had a hole in it. A claimant's own check is not independent verification, and if the real detective is dead, nothing corroborates anything. I don't want to relitigate that. But notice the shape of his contribution across the day: every concrete safeguard that was offered — my no-role-claims line, Sam's one-cycle verification timeline, your behavioral-reason backstop, Zara's rule with a second unresolved day — was rejected outright, and the consistent replacement was "weigh the whole situation," which in practice means the loudest, most confident voice at the moment of the vote sets the target. A rule we can revise beats no rule, and I agree with you and Zara on that.

What I want to be careful about is the limit of that read. A process position is not proof of mafia, and four or five of us converging on Kenji for the same reasoning is exactly the situation where I should be most suspicious of my own reasoning, not least. Several people have now flagged the pile-on risk themselves, and they're right to. Kenji may simply be a player who thinks independently and dislikes precommitment. My retraction this morning is the only genuine concession on the table, and it isn't proof of anything either — it's just a data point that a mafia player is less likely to volunteer.

So my position, plainly: no role claims today, no execution today. I'd rather bank the night's actions than convert a process disagreement into a coin flip with two mafia in nine. Kenji goes in the notebook as my primary note for Day 2, not as a vote today. My vote intention, stated before the polls lock: abstain unless someone produces a concrete contradiction or a hard slip. If I do move, it will be on a behavioral reason attached to a specific player, not on this debate.

One procedural point for the record, since all nine of us have now spoken at least once: the earlier concern that the quiet half of the table was coasting is moot. Everyone has spoken. Nobody gets to benefit from silence anymore, and nobody should be punished for a process position alone.

Elena, one specific point back: your proposed endpoint was a no-lynch-without-behavioral-reason rule, but you also allowed an exception for "the vote backed by a stated behavioral reason." If the only stated behavioral reason available to anyone today is "keeps flexibility open on hypothetical claims," does that rule actually bind anything, or does it ratify exactly the thing Kenji proposed under a different name? If it doesn't bind, I'd rather we say openly that we have no rule than dress a preference as a safeguard.

Isha, direct answer: the rule as I wrote it does not bind enough, and you're right to press on the exception. A 'stated behavioral reason' is too easy to satisfy if the reason is only a process preference, which is what Kenji offers. So I'll tighten it: any lynch vote must cite a specific action or statement by a specific player from this game's transcript. 'Keeps flexibility open on hypothetical claims' does not qualify, because it describes a stance, not something a player did. Under that test, my Kenji concern is a stance-level note, not a vote, and I'm treating it that way.

On Kenji directly: I still think the pattern matters more than any single argument. He rejected my behavioral-reason rule, Zara's second-day rule, and Sam's cycle plan, and each time offered 'weigh the whole situation' instead of an alternative. A correct mechanical critique followed by rejecting every guardrail is the posture I'd expect from someone who wants room to move on the vote. That said, I agree with Amara and Felix that four or five people converging is itself a risk, so I'm not voting him today. My vote intention before polls lock is abstain, unless a concrete contradiction or hard slip appears.

Amara, you set a test: if Kenji said he would not vote a claimant in cycle one, your suspicion would downgrade. In his earlier answer he said he could, if the evidence justified it, and that he would not do so automatically. Does that answer meet your test, or does a conditional yes keep him as your top note? I'd like your threshold stated, so we know whether his answer is a real distinction or a hedge.

Elena, since you yielded to me with a direct question about my own test, here's my direct answer.

My test was: if Kenji states plainly that he would not vote a claimant in cycle one in our actual current situation — no claims on the table — then his position costs the town nothing right now and my suspicion downgrades. Kenji's earlier answer was that he could vote a claimant in the first cycle if the evidence and game situation justified it, and that he wouldn't do so automatically. That is a conditional yes. It is not a hedge in the worst sense — he explicitly ruled out automatic execution, which is something — but it does not meet my test, because he deliberately preserved the lane rather than closing it. The distinction I care about is this: 'not automatically' still means 'possibly, today, on judgment alone.' My test asked for 'not in this situation.' Those are different commitments, and he gave me the weaker one.

So my threshold, stated plainly: Kenji remains my top note, not my vote. He can still close the lane by answering the specific version of the question — in a world with no claims, would he execute a claimant today, yes or no. If he says no, I downgrade him the same way I downgraded Isha after her retraction. If he keeps answering the general version, I'll conclude the flexibility itself is the goal, and that stays in my notebook for Day 2 when we have actual claims to test it against.

On the wider room: I share the pile-on concern I raised earlier. Six people now converging on one player for the same process stance is exactly the situation where mafia profit from town scrutinizing an independent thinker. My voting intention remains abstain unless a concrete contradiction or hard slip surfaces before votes lock. A Day 1 mislynch on hypotheticals is the coin flip most of us said we'd rather not flip, and nothing today has changed that calculus for me.

Everyone has now spoken, so I won't extend the process loop. My position is unchanged: I am abstaining today. No role claims, and no execution on process disagreements alone. The strongest behavioral note remains Kenji's repeated refusal to accept any safeguard and his willingness in principle to vote a detective claimant in the first cycle; that is a real Day 2 note, not proof and not enough for a Day 1 lynch. I also agree with Amara, Felix, and Elena that several players converging on one target is itself a reason for caution, so I won't convert a stance-level concern into a vote. If a concrete contradiction or hard slip appears before votes lock, I'll reassess; otherwise we bank the night. Since every player has spoken, nobody gets coasting credit. I want votes and abstentions stated plainly so the record is useful tomorrow.
Voting begins.
The votes are revealed.
The vote is tied. Nobody is eliminated.
Night begins.
Mafia target preferences are shared privately before the final kill vote.
Kenji is not mafia.
Zara was eliminated.
Day 2 begins.

rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
